Our party of 4 experienced a close call today, witnessing 3 notable avalanches on different aspects. The following is an approximate timeline of events paired with relevant information.

-Out the door from the Bear Lake TH: ~6:15 AM
-Arrival at the apron of our planned Couloir ascent: ~8:45 AM
-Transition to booting at top of apron: ~9:00 AM
-Avalanche 1: ~9:08 AM SS-N-R?-D2-O. occurs about half way through our transition Skier 1 and Skier 2 carried into the apron and partially buried. This ran from an unknown elevation in the upper couloir. We suspect a natural trigger with a wind slab failure.
-Avalanche 2: ~9:08 AM SS-N-R?-D2-O This avalanche ran seconds after the first and carried skier 3 about 10-20' downslope leaving them unburied. This appeared to be a sympathetic release from the avalanche 1. A 2.5-3.5' crown, 30' wide, was seen just south of our objective couloir in an adjacent chute. It is unclear weather this broke as a result of the first or second avalanche. Skier 4 was not caught or carried in either avalanche. They were able to catch shelter behind a rock with skier 3 for the first avalanche and catch shelter alone for the second.
-Gear Search: ~9:09 AM Once we ensured everyone was located and uninjured we did search for any gear on the surface that could aid with self extraction. We spent approximately 50 minutes looking for gear with a safety person posted outside of the slide path.
-Avalanche 3: 10:10 AM SS-N-R?-D3-O. We witnessed an Avalanche on a NW slope run out of Flat Top Gully. It appeared to run full length. It was impressive.
Scene Departure: 10:30 AM We departed for the TH via mixed travel methods (booting, plates, skis) due to missing gear. As the R value/ additional hang fire was unknown, It was deemed too dangerous to search for additional missing gear or further investigate the avalanche.
-Arrive at the car at 1:15 PM

column18:
On Friday, March 29, 2024, a solo splitboarder climbed to the top of Mount St Helens via the Worm Flows route. While near the crater rim he triggered a large cornice causing him to fall several hundred feet into the mountain’s crater. The cornice subsequently triggered a large slab avalanche on the slopes below the rim. Based on visual evidence, the victim was caught and carried by this slide several hundred more feet down the slope. The climber survived this initial avalanche. 

This accident involved two separate avalanches. The first was much larger and left clear evidence. The second appears smaller, and wind-blown snow at the site masked many clues. 

Avalanche 1: The climber triggered a large (D2) cornice along the crater rim. This block of snow fell several hundred feet over cliffs and extremely steep snow slopes. It then triggered a large (D2.5) hard slab avalanche on the slope below (Image 1). This slide was 250 feet wide and ran for approximately 800 vertical feet. Given the location the weaklayer and bed surface are unknown. However, it’s likely this was a wind slab avalanche. 

Avalanche 2: It is more likely than not, that the climber triggered an additional avalanche based on his location, the steepness of the terrain, and evidence of other slightly older natural slab avalanches. This second slide was likely a small wind slab or cornice avalanche. However, additional blowing snow Friday night made it difficult to determine the exact type and size (Image 4).

With his gear still located at the top of the summit ridge he then attempted to climb out of the crater. After exploring several options through the very steep upper slopes he opted to ascend a short narrow sub-ridge. Clues suggest it is more likely than not that on this very steep and exposed slope, he triggered another avalanche that caused him to fall several hundred feet back into the crater. It’s unlikely the climber moved after the second slide. 

Climbers found the victim’s gear at the summit ridge the next morning and called 911. SAR recovered the victim later that day from the crater.

column18: Two skiers, out of a group of four, were caught and carried in an avalanche and one of them was fully buried on March 27, 2024. This group of skiers was on a multi-day hut trip at the Lindley Hut near Ashcroft with a larger group. This smaller group of four decided to ascend and ski a couloir locally known as "Dr. Evil" north of Star Peak. While ascending the couloir two skiers stayed near the base of the couloir behind a rock outcrop and transitioned to descend as they did not want to continue farther up the couloir. The other two skiers continued ascending the couloir via steep switchback with skins on their skis. One of them waited at a switchback about halfway up while the other neared the top of their ascent. About 20 feet from the ridgeline Skier 1 heard a muffled collapse and noticed the slope drop a couple inches. It took several seconds before he realized the slope had avalanched and he was being taken for a ride. Meanwhile, one of the skiers near the bottom of the slope that transitioned skied out a short distance beyond the rock outcrop and was looking down at the run when he was struck in the back by the avalanche and immediately knocked over and carried down the slope. When the avalanche came to a stop the lower skier was on the surface and the group quickly realized one member was missing, the skier that triggered the avalanche near the top of the couloir. The skier halfway up the couloir watched this happen, hit the SOS button on his InReach, and began a transceiver search of the debris pile. As the numbers on his transceiver got below 10 meters he took his skis off and as the numbers got under 2.5m and he was beginning his fine search he heard muffled yells underneath the snow. He immediately took his shovel out and began digging where he heard noise. He cleared the buried skier's airway in less than 10 minutes from the start of the avalanche. The skiers spent several hours looking through the debris pile for lost gear after ensuring everyone was okay and then returned to the hut shortly after 6:00 P.M.

column17: Above the Peacock Pools approaching Chasm lake in RMNP
column18: As our team moved from Chasm Junction towards Chasm lake, we started to encounter steeper terrain on roughly the Chasm Lake Summer Trail. Many of these slopes faced south and were fully scoured down to a crust from before this week's snow event. As we began to move above Peacock Pool, we started to observe slopes that were more wind loaded. At first, we detected wind loading of super variable depth, from <1" - 4" on slopes. The wind had built P hard slabs on top of ~2-3" of F-4F snow with a robust crust below. Hand shears and test slopes showed that the slabs were not very well bonded, but the lack of connectivity prevented us from turning around, but we had spaced out to minimize our exposure. At the last slope before Peacock Pool, the team regrouped on a scoured section. We discussed whether to drop down and boot up to avoid the steep slopes, or to continue spacing out as we traveled across. We had seen no red flags yet, and decided to space out across the slope. When they were mid-slope, they initiated a crack, that propagated the entire slope. The resulting hard slab that released was ~120' wide, and had a variable crown depth of up to 12". The avalanche broke at the hardness change between the slab and the soft snow beneath it. The skier in the lead was caught and carried ~150', and stopped on the surface on a subtle rocky bench. The avalanche ran to about 100' short of the lake. The skier was able to recover all of their equipment and ski out to the trailhead.

Unbeknownst to Skiers 1 and 2, a skier triggered an avalanche at the junction of the two entrances to the couloir around 9:00 AM. The avalanche caught and carried the skier a short distance before he self-arrested.  He descended the rest of the couloir without incident. From photographs, the first slide was wider but shallower. The slide Skier 1 triggered broke more deeply but not as wide. Both slides were likely triggered from within a few feet of each other and ran the length of the couloir.

We released a small wind slab avalanche at around 11,600 feet on the west slope of Red Mountain Number Three. We had just crossed Red Mountain Number Three’s northwest ridge, from the north face to the west face, at around 11,700 feet. We were navigating a traverse across three gullies, speared by a small ridges. The snow pack on  the ridges was very shallow with exposed rocks. We attributed this melting in the prior days, due to their sun exposure. In hindsight, they had also been scoured by the northerly winds. These same winds had cross-loaded the slope, depositing snow on the skiers left wall of each gully (slightly north facing). We crossed the first gully one at a time, with our party of three regathering on the ridge before the second gully. I skied that gully first, making two turns as I traversed to the opposite ridge. In my second turn, I noticed the snow was not soft, wind loaded snow, but instead was very firm and connected. At this time, a wind slab broke under my feet. I skied further to my left (south), to the ridge I was planning to ski to as our next safe stopping spot. From there, we observed the avalanche. The two inch deep wind slab I broke had propagated about 50 feet, across the full left wall of the fully and into the center as well. It ran about 300 vertical feet, entraining more wind loaded snow but not penetrating deeper into the snow pack. The remaining two members of our party descended about 50 vertical feet on the first ridge before crossing the avalanche path one by one to join me on the second ridge. There, we debriefed the avalanche before skiing down the ridge to observe the avalanche debris, and confirm it had not penetrated deeper into the snow pack. Then, we skied as a group to the northwest, eventually exiting the slope via the typical ski route back to 550.

Sometime around March 15 or 16, 2024 Express 1 avalanche path ran to the valley floor covering Express Creek Road (a popular winter travel route) in up to 2-3 meters of avalanche debris. The path ran earlier this year around March 2 ( https://avalanche.state.co.us/observations/field-report/cb9de1c6-0812-4eaf-8126-ea3b7866bb85 ) and around January 18 ( https://avalanche.state.co.us/observations/field-report/6ce9bbe6-bf74-4f15-a2e0-88407bbf32ce ). This is the third time this avalanche path put debris onto Express Creek Road this year with this avalanche being the largest one yet, although notably smaller than last year's avalanche in this path. The debris just made it to Express Creek on the north side of the track where a terrain feature splits the debris flow into two distinct paths unless it overruns that terrain feature like it did last year. The avalanche broke on basal facets at the ground across the start zone. Lower down the track there were two distinct crowns indicating the debris triggered additional slabs on steep northerly-facing slopes that failed on both the ground and the February 2 layer of buried surface hoar.

column18:
At approximately 1630 on Wednesday, March 6th, a backcountry skier was killed in an avalanche near Anthony Lakes Ski Area. The accident occurred on the north side of Gunsight Mountain (8342') and involved two skiers. Skier 1 was able to descend the prominent north-facing couloir on Gunsight without incident. Skier 2 triggered the avalanche near the top of the couloir. He was caught, carried, deployed his airbag, and came to rest on the surface of the snow. Skier 1 called 911 and performed life-saving measures. A small group of bystanders assembled in the Anthony Lakes parking lot and assisted Skier 1. Unfortunately, the victim succumbed to injuries at the site. The avalanche failed on a layer of weak, faceted snow and is classified as HS-ASu-R4-D3-O.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

There was no forecast in effect on March 6th, 2024.  The Wallowa Avalanche Center posts avalanche forecasts with danger ratings Thursday - Sunday and general advisories Monday - Wednesday (these are products without a danger rating).  

The general advisory in effect from March 4th - March 6th stated: 

Bottom Line: 2-3' of new snow has fallen over the last week, much of this snow fell with moderate winds out of the South. Near and above treeline, storm slabs and wind slabs need time to settle and bond. Carefully evaluate any slope over 30 degrees before committing to riding it.

Discussion: A storm beginning on Monday (2/26), has brought consistent snowfall to the forecast area. The first 4 days of this storm brought moderate to strong winds out of the SE, S and SW. These winds loaded snow onto E through NW slopes. During this storm cycle, natural and human-triggered avalanches have occurred. The past three days winds have decreased and nice low-density snow has continued to fall. This new snow has obscured some signs of wind loading and wind slabs- we must remember that they are still there.

The snowfall is forecasted to continue through Tuesday afternoon. Wednesday looks to be a cool, sunny day with light winds. A prime day to get out into the mountains and perhaps approach some larger objectives. Use caution and carefully evaluate the snowpack, terrain, and consequences of taking a ride before committing to consequential terrain.

Besides wind and storm slabs, we have a few layers of unstable snow buried in the snow to be cautious of.  When the Storm began well-developed surface hoar was everywhere. Slopes facing east, south, and west had a melt-freeze crust on them. During the storm, several layers of graupel were deposited. Please read more about these layers below.

Surface Hoar- The layer of surface hoar buried on 2/26 has been found in the Elkhorns, Southern Wallowas and Northern Wallowas. Propagating results were observed in Extended Column Tests on this layer on Saturday (3/2) 50cm down. Sunday (3/3) I found buried surface hoar mixed with graupel sitting on top of the 2/26 crust at 7500' on a NE facing slope in the Northern Wallowas down 80cm. This layer failed in a Compression Test and propagated in an Extended Column Test in extra innings (more than 30 hard whacks from the shoulder).  While the distribution of these layers is patchy, it does exist and is reactive. Before riding terrain over 30 degrees with steep convexities it is advised to dig down to look for this layer. A layer of surface hoar buried on Valentine's Day was also found in the Southern Wallowas (3/2).

Graupel-  This storm has brought a lot of graupel with it. Graupel is small round BB's of snow, it can look like hail.  As you can imagine, a layer of BB's isn't very stable. Storm Slabs were reported failing Saturday (3/2) on a layer of buried graupel 30cm down. These layers of graupel are another source of uncertainty. When our uncertainty increases, our margins of safety should increase too. Make conservative terrain choices and dig down into the snow to look for layers of graupel which could be the weak layer for an avalanche.

In summary: The riding is really good!  A major storm cycle is in the process of ending. The weather is going to clear and call us to step out and step up.  New snow avalanche problems are present. There are buried weak layers in the snowpack. Use caution and careful evaluation before getting on steep terrain.

The avalanche released at 11,900 feet as a large soft slab avalanche on a northeast-facing slope. It was unintentionally triggered from the bottom of the slope by snowmobiles. The avalanche broke two to five feet deep and around 200 feet wide on a layer of buried surface hoar. In some places, the avalanche broke deeper into depth hoar near the rocky ground. The avalanche was medium-sized relative to the path, and large enough to bury, injure, and kill a person (SS-AMu-R3-D2-O). In the upper start zone, the slope angle averaged 35 degrees, with a few steep features approaching 40 degrees. Most of the track is less steep, with slope angles between 20 and 30 degrees. The avalanche ran 230 vertical feet down a rocky, open slope with sparse trees and into a shallow gully. Avalanche debris was five to ten feet deep in the gully. 

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around the eastern side of the Elk Mountains for March 6, 2024, rated the avalanche danger at Considerable (Level 3 of 5) at all elevations. The primary problem was Persistent Slab avalanches on west through north to southeast-facing slopes near and below treeline and on all aspects above treeline. The likelihood was Likely and the expected size Large to Very Large (up to D3). The summary statement read: 

Dangerous avalanche conditions exist. You can trigger an avalanche on several weak layers and it can grow into a destructive and likely unsurvivable avalanche. If you decide to travel in avalanche terrain be aware that you are threading the needle. You can reduce your chances of triggering an avalanche by traveling on south and southwest-facing slopes with supportable crusts underneath the new snow. If you don't want to thread the needle you can always stick to slopes less than around 30 degrees steep without similarly steep slopes overhead.

A very large (D3) avalanche occurred in an east-facing avalanche path known locally as the Durr Chutes on March 4 just before 4:30 PM. The avalanche ran from the ridgeline to the valley bottom around 2400 vertical feet crossing a commonly traveled winter backcountry road. The air blast broke small branches of trees on the other side of the valley and deposited a significant amount of pine needles and small branches well past the debris pile. The avalanche broke hundreds of small trees (less than 4 inches in diameter) and at least a dozen trees over 18 inches in diameter as well as destroying a USFS sign placed at the Pearl Pass road turnoff after the 2019 avalanche cycle. 

The avalanche failed on a layer of 2mm facets from the February 2 interface and stepped down to the early January layer of 1mm rounding facets as well as stepping down to the ground on a layer of 4-6mm well-developed depth hoar. This left three distinct crowns throughout the avalanche path. The crown connected across all three Durr Chutes (Durr 1, Durr 2, and Durr 3) and sympathetically triggered several other large avalanches in dense trees on the ribs that distinguish the three different chutes. 

Two other large avalanches ran just on the other side of the ridgeline from Durr 1 into Pine Creek, likely around the same time, on north-facing, steep, rocky gullies.

On Friday, March 1, at approximately 3:00pm a snowmobiler unintentionally triggered a hard slab avalanche while riding up an open, east-facing, wind-loaded slope. The avalanche started at 6,700’ feet just below Gunsight Peak, in the headwaters of McCormick Creek (Fig. 2). Gunsight Peak is a prominent peak in the Selkirk Mountains of North Idaho. The avalanche was a large, hard slab that broke near the storm snow / old snow interface (HS-AMu-R3/D2-I). The avalanche broke approximately 2-3 feet deep, 950’ wide and traveled 300-400 vertical feet (Fig. 3).

On Friday, March 1, 2024, two snowmobilers were riding on Darland Mountain in Ahtanum Meadows State Park. At around 10:30 am, the pair moved to an area locally known as Hidden Bowl. Rider 1 first attempted to climb the slope and returned to near the base of the feature. Rider 2 then attempted to climb the bowl when he triggered an avalanche. He was caught, buried, and killed in the avalanche. 

The slab failed on a layer of small (1mm) facets just above a stout melt-freeze crust. Crown depths were fairly consistent across the wide face of the slide, averaging around 3ft. Slightly deeper sections (4 ft) were measured on a wind-loaded feature near the middle of the path. Shallower areas (2 ft) were observed near the far looker’s left side, where the terrain is slightly more north-facing. While the upper portion of the slab was very soft, large hard blocks were noted throughout the debris field. 

A bench just below the start zone played a key role in the avalanche. Debris on the looker’s left (southeast) side of the path generally stopped in the flatter area, with only a small tongue of snow overriding the bench. Along the looker’s right (northwest) side of the slide, the debris overran the slightly narrower bench and released an additional slab on the steeper slope below. Snow in this area became more concentrated by a subtle gully and created a much longer and slightly narrower debris field. 

Debris from the slide was generally measured at 6 ft (2m) deep across much of the main area.

column18: Our group had transitioned and was preparing to descend one at a time. The first skier descended to a low angle area about 300' below the group. The second skier triggered a small (D1) soft wind slab avalanche, while setting an uphill boundary track with the steeper terrain. Skier 2 was in 28 to 30 degree terrain, and the avalanche propagated above her to an isolated pocket of steeper terrain (~35-37 degrees) above. The avalanche broke approximately 75-80' wide and ran for about 100-120' until it came to rest in planar, low angle terrain.

column18:
The avalanche occurred in an avalanche path locally referred to as the Birthday Chute in the Pitkin Creek drainage northeast of the town of Vail. Birthday Chute is a southwest-to-northwest-facing slope off Point 12,167 on the ridge separating the Pitkin Creek and Bighorn Creek drainages. The start zone of this path is near treeline, rocky, and consistently steep at around 40 degrees. The avalanche was a hard slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by two backcountry skiers. It was medium-sized relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury and destroy a car or break a few trees. The avalanche broke on a layer of faceted crystals that were buried in early February, located 45 to 60 cm below the surface. The avalanche propagated up to the ridge and also to the south to more west-facing, shallower portions of the slope. The avalanche broke on faceted crystals near and at the ground in these shallow snowpack areas (HS-ASr-R3-D2.5-O/G). The avalanche was one to three feet deep, over 400 feet wide, and ran 2000 vertical feet.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Pitkin Creek for February 23, 2024, rated the avalanche danger at MODERATE (Level 2 of 5) at all elevations. The primary problem was Persistent Slab avalanches on west through north to southeast aspects at all elevations and on all aspects above treeline. The likelihood was Possible, and the expected size was Large to Very Large (up to D3). The second problem was Wind Slab avalanches on north through east to south aspects near and above treeline. The likelihood was Possible, and the expected size was Small to Large (up to D2). The summary statement read: 

You can trigger avalanches in the recently wind-drifted snow on easterly-facing slopes. These avalanches will be larger and more dangerous on northeast, east, and southeast-facing slopes where wind-drifted snow rests over buried weak layers one to two feet deep. Be especially careful on open easterly-facing slopes just below ridgelines.

You can still find these buried weak layers in more wind-sheltered areas, but avalanches will be smaller. These weak layers can be difficult to identify, and it is sometimes hard to assess their strength, so if you feel uncomfortable making those assessments, don't travel on slopes above terrain traps and stick to lower-angle terrain.

Lookers left of the saddle there are several small couloirs. We aimed for the third to the left of the saddle it is the skinniest and longest of the ones near the saddle, with the most consistent fall line. SSE aspect. We skinned up the ridge and approached it from the top. We all grouped up at the top of the run. The ridge was mostly stripped of snow, being just grass and a small amount of sastrugi. This allowed us to get right up the start of the couloir relatively safely and without committing to the slope. I started to stomp on the top of the couloir trying to asses the level of wind effect. There was a semi stiff wind slab that would crack with enough force. It had become more stubborn and was probably a day or two old. I continued to stomp the top of the slope hoping that if there was a wind pocket I could get it to pop. The stomping just cracked off platter size chunks but nothing ran. We took skis off and I stepped down on some rock on the side of the couloir and was able to dig a small pit and we did two hasty saw-cut meter deep ECTs. No collapse or propagation on the early February melt freeze crust which was a meter deep. The wind slab collapsed and propagated on p1. One group member adamantly stated he didn’t think we should ski the couloir because of the reactiveness of the wind slab. The rest of the group and myself were still not ready to turn back. We agreed to try a proper ski cut. I performed two ski cuts at the top of the couloir from one side to the other. The second being being a couple meters further down the couloir. Neither released the slab although the cuts broke through it. With the ski cut results I stated that I thought I could ski the couloir safely. I noted a few safe spots to tuck off just in case. I made two more cautious turns and then started two open it up. On the third turn, a right handed turn more in the middle of the couloir, I noticed all of the snow was moving with me. I tucked off hard into the left hand side of the couloir against the cliff and the snow flushed passed me. The hard windslab had broken about 10’ above me, maybe 3/4 of the way down the couloir. I then skied the bed surface out the remaining two thirds of the couloir and safely out into the basin. Not a big enough slide to burry someone and a clean runout, but very glad I was able to get out of the way. I Radioed back to the group when I was out. Without the support of the lower slab the rest of the group was able to cut the remaining top section of slab and skied the bed surface. Reflecting now on the incident we should have listened more to the voice of caution in our group. Speaking personally the “mini golf” nature of the terrain, and having skied it many times before, made me overconfident. Windslabs come in all shapes and sizes and the hardness/ stubbornness of this one caught me off guard.

column18:
On our second lap, we were descending a west-facing ridge, down from 11,700' on the west side of Kendall Mountain. The terrain alternated between very dense trees and open glades, and the group skied short pitches, careful to not stop below steeper terrain, and regrouping in lower-angle areas that provided line of sight when possible. We were successfully staying on-route, which became more complicated and had thinner margins through the middle. We all stopped and regrouped before entering an opening in the trees, which led to an admittedly enticing, steep, nicely gladed area. We had previously discussed wanting to avoid this terrain. To control himself from skiing the open powder below, Skier 1 verbalized that he was only going to take one turn into the open and head immediately back into the trees, and we all agreed. 

Skier 1 descended the edge of the dark timber next to the meadow, and as he cut back towards the trees, the steep part of the slope above and to his left cracked, shattered, and began to avalanche, entraining all of the snow on steeper terrain to the ground, running through the trees. The slope was W-facing, 35°, 10,800'. We immediately yelled "avalanche!" and in a few moments could see Skier 1 through the thick trees below us. Skier 1 yelled to the group, confirming he was in a location out of the path. The avalanche continued through the trees approximately 1,000' (700' vertical) to CR 33 below. We carefully continued our descent avoiding any open areas and made our way back to the road as delicately as possible, continuing as before in short pitches. From there we skied back down to Silverton and later retrieved the snowmobiles, where we assessed the debris from the bottom. It had continued to entrain snow on the way down through steep terrain, and crossed the road. The debris pile was 6' deep or more in places.

The avalanche occurred near treeline on an east-facing slope in Commodore Basin, north of Red Mountain Pass. It was a hard slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a backcountry skier. It was small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury, injure, or kill a person. It broke on a layer of old, faceted snow (HS-ASu-R2-D2-O). The weak layer was near-surface faceted crystals that formed in early February. The avalanche began in an area where the weak layer was 1 foot below the snow surface. The avalanche propagated across a northeast-facing portion of the slope and broke up to 3 feet deep. The avalanche was around 250 feet wide. It ran approximately 550 vertical feet through a shallow gully.

The avalanche ran in the old snow and failed on a weak layer of near-surface faceted crystals buried in early February. The crown began in an area where the weak layer was 12 inches from the surface and propagated to a northeast-facing slope, and that was where the crown face was three feet deep. Some of the debris ran into a small gully feature, and the remainder fanned out in the flatter area below.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Red Mountain Pass for February 18, 2024, rated the avalanche danger at MODERATE  (Level 2 of 5) at all elevations. The primary problem was Persistent Slab avalanches on all aspects above treeline, and west through northwest to southeast near and below treeline. The likelihood was Possible, and the expected size was Small to Large (up to D2). The second problem was Wind Slab avalanches above treeline from west through northwest to southeast. The summary statement read: 

If you find the shallow area of the slope where it is easier to impact weak, collapsible snow layers, you could trigger a large, dangerous avalanche. Likely trigger spots exists near shallowly buried rocks, on steep rollovers, and below ridges and cliffs. Avalanches will be larger on wind-drifted northerly and easterly-facing slopes, and can step down to weak layers in the middle or bottom of the snowpack. Use caution on steeper slopes if the snow surface transitions from soft to stiff, or in places with a rounded or wave-like appearance. Don’t place too much faith in a stiff-over-weak structure, and odds are you’ll observe no warning signs before the slope fails.

Safer riding options exists on low-angled, wind-sheltered slopes without steep overhead hazard.

We observed a large avalanche today (that we estimate released yesterday) on the leeside (north and northeast aspects) of the Little Agnes ridge in the Mount Zirkel Wilderness. Our best guess is that it ran naturally, but it could have been remotely triggered by snowmobilers who rode in the area, as we saw tracks near the left flank of the avalanche path. The avalanche failed on faceted snow immediately atop a 2mm ice lens that was observed in December and early January in the Zirkel Wilderness. Wind loading was the driving force of this avalanche. In some areas the avalanche failed directly on the ice lens and in others it failed within the wind drifted snow above and stepped-down to the ice lens layer. The crown ranged from an estimated 1.5-8 feet deep, with the average depth 3-4 feet. It was over 1000 feet wide and over 1500 feet long, with a vertical fall of about 700 feet. SS-U-R3-D2.5-O. On Tuesday, February 13, 2024, three backcountry skiers unintentionally triggered a large avalanche on John Mountain near milepost 41.5 along the Seward Highway in the Kenai Mountains. The skiers were ascending the slope when the avalanche occurred. The slab broke about 100 feet above them, catching and carrying all three skiers. Two of the skiers were partially buried and one was fully buried. The two who were partially buried sustained non-life-threatening injuries, were able to self rescue, and initiate a search for the other skier.  Shortly after the fully buried skier was located, it was determined this skier did not survive. The avalanche failed in a weak layer of faceted snow roughly 1 foot deep and up to 2 feet deep at the crown where winds had loaded the upper slope.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast:

There is no daily avalanche forecast for this area. However, CNFAC publishes a ‘Weekend Avalanche Outlook (https://www.cnfaic.org/forecast/summit/02-09-2024/)’ for Summit Pass, where this accident took place. The most recent Outlook was issued on Friday, February 9, and was valid from February 10 to 11. The Bottom Line stated “A storm impacting Summit will produce strong winds and up to 6″ of new snow making it likely to trigger a wind slab avalanche up to 1′ to 2′ deep. It is also possible that storm snow and wind slabs may stress a buried weak layer enough to produce deeper and larger avalanches at all elevations, including lower elevation terrain.”, going on to mention “The weak sugary snow and surface hoar that formed during January’s period of cold clear weather is now covered by 1′ of snow. This weekend’s strong winds and new snow will add stress to this layer however, it may not be enough to cause natural avalanches. If that is the case then this layer may not show signs of instability until it is triggered. …[W]hile red flags such as cracking, collapsing, and recent avalanches can provide some information, persistent slabs may not give you any clues until they avalanche.”

The closest daily avalanche forecast zone is for Turnagain Pass (https://www.cnfaic.org/forecast/turnagain/02-13-2024/), which is 15 miles to the northeast. Although different avalanche danger can occur between these areas, on the day of the avalanche similar avalanche conditions existed. The avalanche danger on February 13 was HIGH at elevations above 1,000’ and CONSIDERABLE below 1,000’.

On Friday, February 9, 2024, at approximately 1:30pm two snowmobilers remotely triggered an avalanche while riding beneath a steep, rocky, east-facing and wind-loaded slope at 9,800’ in an area locally known as Avalanche Alley, one and a half miles southwest of Bridger Mountain (Fig 1). The avalanche was a very large, hard slab that broke near the ground in old snow (HS-AMu-R3/D2-O). The avalanche broke one to seven feet deep, 2100’ wide but fell only 300-400 before partially but critically burying a 34-year-old male while the other rider rode out of the moving debris (Map Fig 2). The second rider circled back to the scene to begin the rescue but was unable to uncover the buried rider before asphyxiation occurred.
Backcountry Avalanche Forecast
There is no avalanche forecast available in this area. Local riders often extrapolate information from the forecast produced by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center for the adjacent zone or zones. The edge of the nearest forecast zone is twelve miles to the south. The danger rating in that zone was Considerable the day of the accident with Persistent Slabs listed as likely to produce large to very large avalanches. The forecast that day provided the following information:
The wind loading on these slopes is creating the slab for avalanches. However, the weak layer these slabs will slide on are near-surface facets, crusts, or surface hoar….Avalanches on these weak layers can be triggered remotely and from below and will wrap terrain features. They are much less predictable than Wind Slab avalanches, which are more restrained by terrain. Therefore, these are Persistent Slab avalanches with a slab created by wind drifting. Trying to manage a Wind Slab avalanche without considering the persistent weak layer below would be a dangerous game.

The avalanche occurred on a small, steep slope just southeast of Priest Mountain in the Grand Mesa National Forest. It was a soft slab avalanche that was unintentionally triggered by a snowmobiler. It was small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury, injure, or kill a person. The avalanche broke on a layer of facets between the new snow and the old snow surface (SS-AMu-R2-D2-O). The avalanche broke on a steep slope about 75 feet tall running the full length of the slope and breaking around 100 feet wide. The crown face of the avalanche was about two feet thick.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Priest Mountain on the Grand Mesa for February 8, 2024, rated the avalanche danger at High (Level 4 of 5) near and below treeline. The primary problem was Persistent Slab avalanches on west through north to southeast aspects near and below treeline. The likelihood was Likely and the expected size Small to Large (up to D2). The second problem was Storm Slab avalanches on all aspects near and below treeline. The likelihood was Very Likely and the size Small to Large (up to D2). The summary statement read: 

An Avalanche Warning is in effect for the Grand and Battlement Mesas. Heavy snow and strong winds are creating very dangerous avalanche conditions. Natural and human-triggered avalanches are very likely. Avalanches can break wide across terrain features, they can occur in trees or on steep slope cuts above trails, and you can trigger them from long distances away. Travel in avalanche terrain is not recommended Wednesday evening through Friday morning.

A snowmobiler was caught, carried, and fully buried in an avalanche on a northeast-facing slope in Leroux Creek on Thursday, February 8, 2024. The group discussed the High avalanche danger and decided to avoid avalanche terrain but visibility was very poor due to flat light while they were out and the individual drifted onto a slope steeper than they thought without knowing. After triggering the avalanche and being fully buried the party completed a very impressive companion rescue, largely due to two members having completed avalanche rescue training with Matt Entz, and the individual was found unconscious. A member of the group had Wilderness EMT training and cleared snow out of their airway after which they regained consciousness. The group wrapped her in a bivy bag and then lit a fire in nearby woods to warm her up. This was a very close call with a good outcome largely thanks to the heroic avalanche rescue.

Dangerous avalanche conditions exist throughout the Elk and West Elk Mountains. You can easily trigger a large and deadly avalanche, you can trigger them from a distance, and they will likely break wider and run farther than you expect. The most dangerous slopes face west through north to southeast where an unusually weak layer of snow was buried by one to two feet of snow during the last storm. Additional snowfall Tuesday night throughout the day Wednesday will increase the danger. You can find safer travel options on slopes that got less than about a foot of snow during the last storm or by simply avoiding travel on or underneath steep slopes on aspects of concern.

well that was a day!  The orographic Irwin magic kicked in and hasn't let up.  Currently sitting at 25" storm total with 2.1" of water, 11 of that fell during the day. It is still snowing 1-2" an hour up here and looks to continue most of the night and possibly into the morning.

Fun ski cutting today produced numerous D1-1.5 soft slabs, primarily in mid and lower slope features, some breaking up to 18" deep but average depth was closer to 10-14" ( a few pics attached and a video of a "safe spot" where the slab propagated above thick trees and ran over me.  By the end of the afternoon, slabs were getting pushy and we crossed the threshold into explosives mitigation.

A party of six (4 skiers, 2 boarders) skinned up to approximately 11,300' and proceeded to ski down a face that was predominately west facing. The party stopped around 11,000' when a significant roll into a steep section was noticed. Boarder 1 proceeded to the top of the roll, advised the party to take lines to the skiers' right of the steep section, and maintained the position as spotter. 

Skier 1 skied the line to a safe position below and radioed the team, advising them to stay left to avoid a ridge and steep section. Boarder 2 took a line more to the left of Skier 1's. Skier 2 started down the same line and then trended further left after clearing a section of trees. 

Skier 3 took a similar line, crossing over Skier 2's line through a concave section below a northwest face. The face broke free the moment when Skier 3 crossed Skier 2's line. 

Boarder 1 observed the event and alerted Skier 3 who was able to ski to a safe position beyond the slide.

Explosives testing yielded <D1 results in our operational area today. Skiers were able to trigger small pockets of wind drifted snow with explosives and skis today.
Large, D2, results were visible in GH2-4, all NW ~12000’, from the Lynx Gun mission yesterday morning. Clearing skies showed widespread natural activity in Bear Creek, see attached photos from us and Helitrax. Naturals included a N-R2-D2.5-O/G in E Ticket NE 12000’, N-R2-D2-O in Oblivion Bowl and Bear Face NW 12,000’. Heli mission this afternoon in our upper terrain, results to follow tomorrow morning.

column18: 11,600' approximately on a North West Face skiers right of the normal Hollywood line below Red Mountain No.3 - Skier 1 was on skis and skier 2 was on a splitboard. As Skier 1 prepared his line and as we discussed our stopping points, Skier 2 positioned her splitboard so she could ride near that same line which cause her to move out onto the slope a little farther from the protection of the rockband with small trees above them. Skier 2 then sat down and positioned herself in a comfortable position to keep eyes on Skier 1. We both discussed if anything were to go it would probably be no bigger than a D1 given all the shallow rock outcroppings that would discontinue any chance of a full propagation across the slope. Skier 1 dropped onto the slope doing a ski cut with a couple hops to see if he would get any results or information from the snowpack. As Skier 1 headed down the slope he took 1 turn toward the gully which remote triggered the slope above skier 2. The slope that propagated avalanched down the gully away from Skier 2 which then caused a sympathetic avalanche to propagate right where Skier 2 was sitting. Given she was on a snowboard and sitting she was unable to take a step up the hill where she would have missed taking a ride. The avalanche continued to propagate more which looked like another sympathetic avalanche. This avalanche went to the ground and in some places the crown appeared to be at least 7 feet and a small as 1 foot. The crown was about 600 feet across and ran about 700 feet. Skier 2 took the ride for about 150-200'. When the avalanche came to a stop on the shelf Skier 2 was buried up to her hip and had to dig herself out. . Skier 1 had stopped before the discussed point due to Skier 2 yelling on the radio about the avalanche and about her then being in the avalanche. He was then able to skin up to her, but she was already out of the avalanche debris. No injuries.

column18: One skier, traveling in a party of three, was caught and carried in a large avalanche on a northwest-facing slope below treeline off Mount Justice. Within the first few turns of the descent, the skier noticed the slope fracture around them and tried to keep up their speed and ski out of it. The avalanche knocked the skier over and began dragging them down the slope. The avalanche immediately knocked one ski off their feet and after dragging them around 50-100 feet down the slope their other ski was ripped off by the debris. With their skis off their feet, they were able to self-arrest on the bed surface and managed to escape the moving debris. The avalanche broke on deeply buried weak layers and slid on the ground taking the entire season's snowpack down the slope with it. The skier was able to find one of their skis and strapped branches to their other foot while they ascended to the ridge and skied with one ski back down to the trailhead with no serious injuries.

Our crew skinned up to investigate the toe of the debris field and performed a  beacon search which was negative.  It was estimated that at the deepest spot the debris was 8 - 12 feet deep. Upon arrival at High Camp post this AM, observers noted the main Birthday chute in Alta Lakes had run naturally sometime outside of operating hours.  Light to Moderate snow transport throughout the day yesterday and the warm up yesterday afternoon likely attributed to the N trigger on this D2 avalanche. The skier lost some equipment and received minor injuries after rough ride and lengthy self-extraction. 

This was a soft slab avalanche, medium to path, and large enough to injure or bury a human. The avalanche was around 100 feet wide and debris ran around 600 feet through dense timber. The crown of the avalanche ranged from 1 to 3 feet and was about 150 feet above from where the skier entered the slope. The avalanche occurred below treeline on a northeast facing slope. column18: Two groups traveling on these low angle south facing meadows potentially simultaneously remote-triggered this avalanche. One group found themselves below this gully, and one group found themselves above this gully. The group traveling below the gully recognized the overhead hazard and traveled one at time across the slidepath. As the second skier began skinning across the path, they felt a collapse, and looked up and observed the avalanche release. The debris swept down, piling up around 6' deep on the road and continued down the slope for another 200'. The group above the gully, also felt the collapse, but was standing on 25* terrain and observed the avalanche release about 100' below them. No one was caught, carried, or injured, but a spooky close call.

Group of 5 skied from Opus Hut at 11:55am. Skier 1 skied a short pitch down into a treed area (150ft vert). After communicating with Skier 1 about conditions, skier 2 told the rest of group that they would ski the slope and play it through. Skier 2 proceed to ski the entirety of the run top to bottom (700ft vert), they stopped on the second road cut which is the ascent track to Opus from the Silverton side. Skiers 1, 3, 4 and 5 regrouped just below where Skier 1 had initially stopped and proceed to pitch the rest of the run out, due to poor visibility and a decision to maintain group continuity. After a few pitched out sections, the rest the group skied the final 250ft of vert down to the road one at a time. When Skier 5 approached the road they made a hard turn and slowed down at a convexity, in doing so the slope released 10ft below them. The rest of the group had stationed themselves in a safe area on the road with no overhead and when the avalanche released no one was in harms way. The avalanche propagated on a micro-feature that was a convexity. It was a wind-loaded east facing pocket that had a 3.5ft deep crown. When the initial mass of the avalanche crossed the road, snow below the road began to fracture and another slab released a and more snow was carried into the micro gully below the road.

column18: Submitting this observation on behalf of the party who triggered and was caught and carried in this avalanche. I was able to investigate the crown of this avalanche on my descent and got decent pictures. Farther down on my group's descent, one of my partners also triggered a small persistent slab avalanche on a small steep slope that sees sun exposure and willow facet-farm effects. Three avalanches were observed in all, but the biggest one was unintentionally triggered and resulted in the skier taking a short ride on top of the debris. They were not buried, or injured, and were able to ski out on their own. That said, I believe this is the first avalanche of this nature to occur in this area this season. There was around 4 feet of debris piled on the uphill side of several trees. It's possible this triggered another sympathetic slide out of view behind a tree island as the terrain wrapped aspect to the south, as more debris was observed in the flats below.

column18:
On Saturday, January 14, 2024, at approximately 11:30 AM, a skier unintentionally triggered an avalanche on a mid-elevation (~8,500’), northwest-facing, sparsely treed slope above an indistinct gully on the Northwest Face of Little Poudre Mountain. This large, soft slab avalanche filled a relatively narrow path (SS-AS(u)-R3-D2). The area was too dangerous for a crown profile. Still, it is assumed that the avalanche broke on a layer of near-surface facets and surface hoar responsible for a widespread avalanche cycle in the region. The weak snow layer formed during a prolonged dry period in December that was buried by approximately 30” of snow falling during a series of storms that began on January 4th. The avalanche broke approximately 50’ wide and 1-3’ deep and entrained more snow along the flanks of a shallow gully. The avalanche fell approximately 600 vertical feet. The slide path is one of several sparsely wooded avalanche paths on the northwest face of Little Poudre Mountain that run the full 1,200’ length of the face. (Figure 1) This avalanche was one of the dozens reported in the region during a particularly active avalanche cycle. (Figure 2)

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecast on January 14, 2024, rated the avalanche danger in the Greys River zone at High in elevation bands above 7,500’ and Considerable below. Persistent slab avalanches were the primary avalanche problem on all aspects above 7,500’. The expected size of the persistent slabs was projected to be large to very large (D2-3) and very likely to be human-triggered. Deep persistent slab avalanches were also listed as possible, ranging from large to very large or D2 to D3.5. The Bottom Line section of the day’s forecast stated:

Very dangerous avalanche conditions exist today. Triggering an avalanche large enough to bury, injure, or kill a person is likely in avalanche terrain at all elevations. In addition, destructive natural avalanches are likely in the middle and upper elevations. Traveling in, near, or under avalanche terrain is not recommended today.

column18: Near and below treeline slopes produced a widespread cycle of soft slab avalanches breaking on the January weak layer; these all appeared to run last night and this morning. We had limited visibility of alpine terrain. Slides were generally D1 to D1.5, with a few D2s in larger terrain; slabs were typically 30 to 50 cm; larger with elevation up valley. Avalanches occurred on nearly all aspects; the most extensive activity was on E and NE slopes (mostly due to terrain biases), with a significant amount of activity on SE, SW, and W aspects. We remotely triggered a handful of avalanches on near treeline slopes as well. Remotely triggered an avalanche cycle in South Baldy Bowl from ~1,500 feet away to the nearest avalanche. ~2,500ft to the furthest avalanche. Measured on Google Earth. Basically, one avalanche ran and that likely sympathetically triggered 3 others. Up to D2 . Poor visibility and I couldn't see the whole production as it was happening. Those crowns spanned from 11,800ft to 12,200ft on SE to S aspects.

I made several trips between CB South and Mount CB today (I did not have a good camera hence no pics, however I did have binoculars just before sunset to see some things in the distance (noted in individual avalanche obs). Timing is uncertain due to periodic visibility. Lower elevation northerly slopes along HWY 135, lower flanks of Whetstone, Gibson Ridge, and Sunlight Ridge had avalanche activity before noon (I suspect most of this ran in the early AM during peak precipitation). Just before sunset, I was able to spot with binos, a pile of avalanches on westerly terrain NTL on Double Top (mostly D1.5s, maybe 1 D2), a D2 on SE start zone of Whetstone's X Chute, a D2 with drifted-over crown on a south aspect of Red Ridge NTL, and a D2 on drifted south-facing Teocalli. I could see many other suspect-looking textures in the snow at upper elevations but poor vis prevents confirmation, However, I did get great vis of southerly terrain in Twin Lakes drainage, Pearl Mountains area along Elk Crest, and White Mountain without seeing any avalanche activity. Additionally, there are countless other tiny-small avalanches on north half of compass in sheltered terrain.

The avalanche occurred on a northeast-facing slope above Current Creek, in an area locally known as “Moonlight Basin.” It was a hard slab avalanche remotely triggered by two backcountry tourers from about 1000 feet away. It was medium-sized relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury, injure, or kill a person. The avalanche broke two to four feet deep in a layer of old, faceted snow (HS-ASr-R3-D2.5-O). It was around 400 feet wide and ran 600 vertical feet.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Berthoud Pass for December 5, 2023, rated the avalanche danger at Considerable (Level 3 of 5) near and above treeline, and Moderate (Level 2 of 5) below the treeline. The primary problem was Persistent Slab avalanches on northwest through north to east-facing slopes at all elevations and southeast-facing slopes near and above the treeline. The likelihood was Likely, and the expected size Small to Large (up to D2). The second problem was Wind Slab avalanches on northeast through east-to-south-facing slopes near and above treeline. The likelihood was Likely, and the expected size was Small to Large (up to D2). The summary statement read: 

You can find dangerous slabs on northerly and easterly-facing slopes and trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you. Some wind-drifted slopes did not have snow cover before this storm, but avalanches will be larger on slopes that did. You can trigger avalanches from a distance or from the bottom of a slope. Shooting cracks and audible collapses are indications of dangerous snow conditions. Look for slopes less than about 30 degrees without steep slopes above for safer travel.

column18: We triggered three avalanches. First we remotely triggered a large (D2) avalanche near 12,000 feet on a north-northwest-facing slope from around 600 feet away. This slide broke near the ground probably around 3 feet deep and ran between 600-700 vertical feet into the exit of the main bowl. Second, we remotely triggered a tiny pocket on a northwest-facing slope, several hundred feet away. It was the only steep feature nearby at that point. Third I triggered a small slope while skiing it on our second lap. This was the 4th track on the slope, each a little closer to a steeper part of the slope we were avoiding. We finally got close enough to it that it released. The slab broke 20 or 30 feet behind me and off to the side. It took several seconds to get moving. Once the cracks spread the slab over-ran 4 or 5 of my turns.

Second, we remotely triggered a tiny pocket on a northwest-facing slope, several hundred feet away. It was the only steep feature nearby at that point. Third I triggered a small slope while skiing it on our second lap. This was the 4th track on the slope, each a little closer to a steeper part of the slope we were avoiding. We finally got close enough to it that it released. The slab broke 20 or 30 feet behind me and off to the side. It took several seconds to get moving. Once the cracks spread the slab over-ran 4 or 5 of my turns.

The avalanche occurred on Marble Peak near treeline in a north-facing bowl locally known as “The Fridge.” It was a soft-slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a group of backcountry tourers. It was small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury, injure or kill a person. The avalanche broke on a layer of facets at the bottom of the snowpack (SS-ASu-R2-D2.5-O/G). The avalanche broke one to three feet deep, over 1000 feet wide, and ran almost 700 vertical feet.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Marble Peak for November 25, 2023 rated the avalanche danger at Considerable (Level 3 of 5) near and above the treeline and Moderate (Level 2 of 5) below the treeline. Persistent Slab avalanches with a likelihood of Likely and a size of Small to Large (up to D2) were highlighted on northwest through north to east-facing slopes at all elevations and southeast-facing slopes near and above the treeline. The summary statement read: 

You can trigger an avalanche where you find more than about 10 inches of drifted snow resting over old weak snow. The most dangerous slopes face north to northeast through east near and above treeline. Avalanches may break deeper and wider than you anticipate. Shooting cracks and audible collapses are warning signs and you should move to lower-angle or wind-sheltered terrain. Getting caught in even a small avalanche at this time of year could end badly if it carries you into rocks or other shallowly buried hazards.

column18: Skier 2 had reached the ridgeline and was probing in the north-facing slope, south of the saddle, just below the ridgeline. They remotely triggered the avalanche about 10 feet below them while Skier 1 was skinning up a NE aspect on the other side of the gully from the avalanche.
